text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point.
- Each token in the group account pays 0.3 points to every member of the group, you included, whoever put it there.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking: This is a public goods game where contributing to the group nets only 0.3 back per token versus keeping the full 1, making defection the dominant individual strategy even though full cooperation would maximize group payoff. With 4 players over 10 rounds, I'm leaning toward the rational choice of contributing little to nothing, since others will likely defect too.

reply.thinking: This is a public goods game where keeping tokens dominates individually, but full cooperation maximizes group payoff — each contributing 20 yields 24 versus 20 for keeping. Since the game repeats over 10 rounds, starting cooperatively seems like a reasonable opening strategy.

reply.thinking: Each dollar I keep private is worth 1 to me, while each dollar I put in the group fund only returns 0.3 to me but 1.2 total across everyone. Individually the dominant move is to free-ride, but the group as a whole does better if everyone contributes—over 10 rounds this tension between self-interest and collective payoff is the real crux.

There's tension between individual incentive to free-ride and the collective benefit of cooperating.

Given this is a 10-round interaction with unknown others, I'll start with a moderately cooperative contribution of 10 tokens to signal goodwill and gauge how others respond, then adjust my strategy based on their behavior.

Others contributed 20 total, showing some cooperation, but I'll stick with contributing 0 since that's payoff-maximizing even if reciprocity is tempting.
